For trustees, the transition predictor was the partner's investment, I t+1 , on the next round:
For investors, the transition predictor was the participant's net earnings on the current round, PnL t = return t -investment t :
The trustee equations are presented using CC-referenced indicators; the fitted models used equivalent -1/ + 1 coding of the binary BPD and AD factors.
Investor HMMs included only CC and BPD participants, with CC as the reference.
The coefficients describe baseline transition probabilities, the effect of the trial-level predictor, group differences, and group-by-predictor differences.
The denominator makes the probabilities across all possible next states sum to one.
Initial state probabilities depended on first-round investment for trustees and were constant across investor sequences.
Investor and trustee HMMs used the same multistart search and fit-validity criteria.
For each state count and model family, we screened 20 randomized statemembership starts for 20 iterations and continued the 3 highest-likelihood candidates for up to 2000 iterations.
We also fitted a structured start that placed the starting state means evenly across the feasible response range.

Diagnosis-dependent models were additionally fitted from warm starts based on the highest-likelihood and structured diagnosis-free fits, with the new diagnostic-group coefficients initially set to zero. 5 small perturbations were fitted around each of the structured diagnosis-dependent and structured warm starts.
If no candidate passed the validity criteria, up to 4 additional rounds continued the best finite candidates.

A fit was retained only if the fitting algorithm reported convergence, all likelihoods and parameters were finite, every response distribution had non-zero spread, and every state accounted for at least 0.5% of the total posterior state probability across trials.
This final requirement excluded effectively unused states.
Among the valid candidates, we retained the fit with the highest log likelihood.
States were then ordered by mean return proportion for trustees and mean investment for investors.
At the selected state count, the diagnosis-free model was nested within the diagnosisdependent model because it could be obtained by constraining the group coefficients to zero.
Standard likelihood-ratio theory applies to such fixed-state nested HMM comparisons under regularity conditions, but not to comparisons that change the number of hidden states (Giudici et al., 2000).

text.text: As a robustness check, we refit the diagnosis-relevant mixed models on the subset with valid age and binary gender data (Male/Female only), adding centered age and gender as additive covariates.
These analyses were not part of the primary model-selection procedure and are intended to assess whether the main diagnostic patterns are materially altered by available demographic imbalance.
Because the AD investor subgroup remained small even in the matched sample, investor sensitivity analyses should be interpreted descriptively.

For encouragement, both demographic models retained the participant-specific random-intercept structure used in the primary analysis, so that only the addition of age and gender differed between the matched-sample fits.
For contrast-based sensitivity analyses, we report both raw and Holm-adjusted p-values.

Investor sensitivity to lagged returns remained stable on the matched complete-case sample: the BPD attenuation term was nearly unchanged before (-0.137, 95% CI [-0.213, -0.061], raw p < .001) and after demographic adjustment (-0.139, 95% CI [-0.215, -0.063], raw p < .001), whereas the AD interaction remained null in both specifications.
text.formatted: Investor sensitivity to lagged returns remained stable on the matched complete-case sample: the BPD attenuation term was nearly unchanged before (-0.137, 95% CI [-0.213, -0.061], raw p < .001) and after demographic adjustment (-0.139, 95% CI [-0.215, -0.063], raw p < .001), whereas the AD interaction remained null in both specifications.

text.text: For trustees, the centered AD vs CC contrast in the return model attenuated slightly on the matched sample but remained positive before (0.404, 95% CI [0.068, 0.741], raw p = .018, Holm-adjusted p = .037) and after adjustment (0.391, 95% CI [0.054, 0.728], raw p = .023, Holm-adjusted p = .046), while BPD vs CC remained null.

For the trustee tactical results, encouragement was not robust to restriction to participants with complete demographic data: the AD vs CC contrast was already non-significant on the matched sample before adjustment (OR = 1.475, 95% CI [1.04, 2.09], raw p = .029, Holm-adjusted p = .058) and remained nonsignificant after adjustment (OR = 1.483, 95% CI [1.05, 2.10], raw p = .027, Holm-adjusted p = .053).
Coaxing remained nominal/non-significant in both matched-sample specifications.

Data were collected across three administration modes: in-person behavioural testing (BEH), testing during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and online testing (WEB).
Administration mode was unevenly distributed across diagnostic groups and roles.
In particular, 523 of 540 AD trustees were tested online, whereas all 16 AD investors were tested in person in the behavioural setting.

We also examined whether the central AD-BPD trustee hidden-state findings persisted when the comparison was restricted to the administration mode shared by both groups and when age and gender were included as covariates.

These were post-estimation sensitivity analyses: hidden states were obtained from the validated five-state model fitted to the full trustee sample, after which probability-weighted cooperative-state occupancy, decoded transition outcomes, and model-implied long-run cooperation were compared in the restricted or adjusted samples.

Thus, the online-only analyses address whether the observed administration-mode difference alone accounts for the second-stage group contrasts; they do not remove differences in recruitment or diagnostic ascertainment.
For long-run cooperation, we first analysed all online trustees (n = 686).
We then analysed the online participants with complete age and gender data (n = 600), both before and after demographic adjustment.
Using the same participants for these two analyses separated the effect of adjustment from the effect of excluding participants with missing demographic data.
An additional demographic-adjusted analysis included participants from all testing settings with complete demographic data (n = 806; Table S34).

text.text: The five-state definitions, state-specific return distributions, and posterior state probabilities remained fixed at their full-sample estimates.
Transition models were re-estimated within each analysis sample, including diagnosis, investment, and their interaction; adjusted models additionally included age and gender.
Adjusted predictions at investments of 5, 10, and 15 tokens used the full sample's observed mean age.
Gender-specific long-run cooperative-state probabilities were averaged using the analysis sample's pooled gender proportions, with identical weights across diagnostic groups.
Each analysis used 10,000 successful transition-bootstrap samples, percentile 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided bootstrap tests, following Section S1.3.
Holm correction covered nine comparisons per analysis: three diagnostic-group pairs at three investment levels.
The AD-BPD difference persisted when analysis was restricted to online trustees.
AD trustees had 22.2 percentage points greater probability-weighted cooperative-state occupancy than BPD trustees (95% CI [14.8, 29.6]; Holm-adjusted p < .001).

text.text: At 15 tokens, the difference was not significant in any of these analyses (smallest Holm-adjusted p = .452).
At 10 tokens, the difference in the matched online sample was 24.1 percentage points (95% CI [13.5, 30.7]) before adjustment and 23.4 points (95% CI [12.0, 30.1]) after adjustment.

Among comparisons involving controls, only one survived Holm correction: in the all-settings adjusted analysis, long-run cooperation at 5 tokens was 13.6 points lower in BPD than in CC (95% CI [-24.1, -4.2], Holm-adjusted p = .024).

text.text: Holm adjustments used 18 retention-and-repair comparisons, 18 comparisons across exits to States 1 and 2, and nine long-run cooperation comparisons.
To examine whether the findings depended on the number of hidden states, we repeated the occupancy and transition analyses using neighbouring four-and six-state diagnosis-dependent models.
In each model, the state closest to returning one third of the tripled investment was classified as neutral.
Lower-return states were classified as exploitative and higher-return states as cooperative.
This defined States 3-4 as cooperative in the four-state model and States 4-6 in the six-state model.
The AD-BPD difference was the most consistent result.
AD trustees occupied cooperative states more often than BPD trustees in both alternative models.
They also showed greater long-run cooperation at every investment level in the four-state model and at 10 and 15 tokens in the six-state model.
Repair after exploitation was also higher in AD than BPD at every investment level in the four-state model and at 10 and 15 tokens in the six-state model.
The BPD-CC transition pattern depended on the number of states.
In the six-state model, BPD trustees showed lower cooperative retention than controls at 5 and 10 tokens after adjustment; the difference at 15 tokens did not remain reliable.
The four-state model showed no reliable BPD retention deficit and instead identified lower BPD repair at 10 and 15 tokens.

Thus, the AD-BPD occupancy difference was stable and the long-run cooperation difference held at most investment levels, whereas whether BPD-CC differences appeared in cooperative maintenance or repair depended on how finely behaviour was divided into states.

AD trustees showed higher repair than controls at 5 and 10 tokens in the four-state model; the remaining AD-CC repair comparisons, including all comparisons in the six-state model, did not remain reliable after adjustment.
In the six-state model, AD retention was lower than that of controls at 10 tokens.

Beyond mean investment amounts and return proportions, we derived behavioural features capturing dynamic reciprocity patterns and strategic adjustment.
While these can be summarised as participant-level proportions for descriptive purposes, our primary analysis treated them as binary outcomes in trial-level generalised linear mixed models (GLMMs).
Diagnostic groups were community controls (CC), participants with borderline personality disorder (BPD), and affective-symptom service users (AD).
Descriptive proportions used the opportunity conditions below.
Trial-level models additionally applied the stated eligibility conditions to exclude rounds in which the response was impossible.
All trial-level models used rounds with the required previous-round information and observed outcomes, excluding the first round.
Fair Return Benchmark We defined a "fair return" as the amount equalising payoffs between investor and trustee: fair_return = 2 × investment -10 if investment ≥ 5 0 otherwise
When investment < 5, any positive return exceeds fairness because the tripled amount is insufficient to equalise payoffs.
text.formatted: When investment < 5, any positive return exceeds fairness because the tripled amount is insufficient to equalise payoffs.

text.text: For example, if investment is 0, the trustee receives 0, and if investment is 1, the trustee receives 3, such that any return leaves unequal totals.
Investor Behavioural Features Responsiveness: Modelled as a binary event on trials following betterthan-fair returns.
* Opportunity Condition: return t-1 > fair_return t-1 * Additional Model Eligibility: investment t-1 < 20, so investment could increase.

Figure 1: Investor behaviour by diagnostic group.

Panel A shows trial-level investment distributions by diagnosis, with coloured violins and white boxplots summarising trial-level observations and overlaid points showing participant-level mean investments across the 10 rounds.

Panel B shows model-predicted next-round investment as a function of lagged net return (prior-round profit) for CC and BPD investors, holding other predictors at their centered means; shaded ribbons show 95% confidence intervals and the dashed vertical line marks the break-even point.
The vertical axis is restricted to the feasible 0-20-token investment range; fitted values outside this range are not displayed.

This conditional comparison differs from comparing each participant's returns across the whole game.
Raw focal contrasts are shown for transparency; Holm adjustment did not change the inferential status of these contrasts.
Figure2: Trustee return behaviour by group.
Panel A shows trial-level return-proportion distributions as coloured violins and white boxplots; overlaid points show participant-level means across the 10 rounds.
Panels B-D show GLMM-predicted probabilities, with points indicating predicted probabilities and vertical bars 95% confidence intervals.
Panel B shows coaxing, defined as returning at least the invested amount after a low but non-zero investment.
Panel C shows encouragement, defined as returning more tokens than in the preceding round when the investor sent fewer.
Panel D shows cooperation pick-up, defined as returning more tokens when the investor sent more.
Colours denote group.
Brackets and asterisks mark CC-referenced contrasts that remained significant after Holm correction.
Figure3: Investor HMM state profiles and diagnostic occupancy.
Panel A shows the fitted investment distribution for each state.
Panel B shows, for each diagnostic group, the proportion of investor trials assigned to each state in the most-likely-state analysis.
Error bars show participant-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 draws), conditional on the fitted state assignments.
States are ordered from lower to higher investment.
Brackets and asterisks mark CC-BPD differences that remained significant after Holm correction across states.
Figure 5: Fitted trustee HMM transition metrics by diagnosis across three partner-investment levels, with 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 bootstrap samples.
Points show estimated probabilities, vertical bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and colour/shape identify diagnosis.

Panels display (A) repair, the probability of moving from exploitative State 1 into cooperative States 3-5; (B) cooperative retention, the probability of remaining in States 3-5; (C) exploitative exit, the probability of leaving States 3-5 for State 1; and (D) model-implied long-run cooperation, the eventual probability of occupying States 3-5 if the displayed partner investment continued across rounds.
Brackets and asterisks mark Holm-adjusted pairwise contrasts that are significant at a given investment level.
FigureS1: Full transition functions from the selected 5-state trustee hidden Markov model.
Rows indicate the current state and columns indicate the possible next state.
Within each panel, lines show the fitted probability of that transition across following-round partner investments from 0 to 20 tokens.
States are ordered from lower-to higher-return policies; line colour denotes diagnostic group.
